clinicalPearls: Benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar and digital fascia producing nodules, cords and progressive flexion contracture, most often of the ring and little fingers.

Strong association with northern European ancestry, positive family history, male sex and increasing age; alcohol misuse, diabetes mellitus, smoking and antiepileptic therapy are recognised associations.

The pathological cord contracts the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; MCP contracture is more readily corrected than PIP contracture, which tends to be more resistant and prone to recurrence.
A positive Hueston tabletop test (inability to lay the palm flat on a flat surface) is a useful clinical indicator that intervention should be considered.
Dupuytren diathesis (early onset, bilateral disease, strong family history, ectopic lesions) predicts aggressive behaviour and higher recurrence.
Ectopic disease includes knuckle pads (Garrod nodes), plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease) and penile fibromatosis (Peyronie disease).

Treatment options include limited fasciectomy, percutaneous needle fasciotomy and collagenase clostridial injection; choice balances contracture severity, joint involved, patient fitness and recurrence risk.
Recurrence is common regardless of technique, and the condition is controlled rather than cured; realistic counselling about recurrence and the aim of function is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative condition in which myofibroblasts within the longitudinal palmar and digital fascia proliferate and deposit disorganised type III collagen. Progression classically passes through a proliferative nodular phase rich in contractile myofibroblasts, an involutional phase in which cords align along lines of tension, and a residual phase of relatively acellular collagenous cord. Dysregulated cytokine signalling, particularly transforming growth factor beta and platelet-derived growth factor, together with local oxidative stress and a genetic predisposition involving Wnt signalling pathway variants, drives contraction of the diseased fascia and secondary joint contracture.
additionalDifferentials: Stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger) with a palpable nodule
Soft-tissue sarcoma or other palmar mass
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is rarely required
Serial goniometric measurement of MCP and PIP contracture angles
Ultrasound to characterise an atypical palmar mass when the diagnosis is uncertain
MRI reserved for suspected sarcoma or atypical rapidly enlarging lesions
Screening for associated diabetes mellitus where clinically indicated
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging, painful or firm fixed mass suggesting sarcoma rather than benign fibromatosis
Progressive fixed PIP flexion contracture threatening hand function
Skin ulceration, maceration or fixed web-space contracture impairing hygiene
Sensory or vascular compromise of a digit from severe contracture
reference.prognosis: A benign but chronic and progressive condition that is controlled rather than cured, with recurrence common after any intervention, particularly in patients with a strong diathesis. Function is generally well preserved with appropriate timing of treatment, though established PIP contractures respond less predictably.
pitfalls: Mistaking a Dupuytren nodule for a trigger finger nodule or a ganglion and mismanaging it
Operating too early on a soft palmar nodule without contracture, exposing the patient to surgical risk for little functional gain
Underestimating the difficulty and recurrence rate of correcting fixed PIP contractures
Failing to recognise digital neurovascular bundle displacement by spiral cords, risking iatrogenic injury during fasciectomy
Overlooking diathesis features that should temper prognostic expectations
references: British Society for Surgery of the Hand guidance on Dupuytren disease
management: Monitor nodular or non-disabling disease, intervening when a functionally significant contracture develops or the Hueston tabletop test becomes positive
Treat a defined cord with minimally invasive options such as percutaneous needle fasciotomy or collagenase clostridium histolyticum injection followed by cord manipulation
Perform limited fasciectomy for significant joint contracture, counselling that proximal interphalangeal contractures are more resistant and recurrence-prone than metacarpophalangeal ones
Reserve dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin grafting for recurrent disease or those with a marked diathesis
Deliver structured hand therapy with night extension splinting after intervention and take care to protect the neurovascular bundle displaced by a spiral cord
Optimise associated conditions including diabetes mellitus and hazardous alcohol and tobacco use
Counsel that the condition is controlled rather than cured and follow up for recurrence, especially with an aggressive diathesis
